title.title: Is federal contract money going to fewer companies?
title.subtitle:
A first look at the civilian agencies, FY2008 to FY2025
Suchitra Hole, Shivram Nekkanti, Andy Hannah  |  October 2026
title.notes: Our project asks a simple question: when the government buys something, does the money go to many companies or to a few? Today: the data, how we processed it, how we measure it, and what the first look shows for the civilian agencies.

question.title: The question: many companies, or a few?
question.goal: Our goal: for every civilian agency, product and year, measure whether the money is spread out or goes to a few companies.
question.takeaway: When a few companies win most of an agency's money, the government has less choice and less price pressure. A high score is not wrongdoing: some work only one firm can do.
question.notes: Civilian agencies, everything except Defense, spent about 301 billion dollars on contracts in FY2025. Defense spent another 492 billion, but it buys from a handful of large weapons makers and already studies its own market, so we focus on the civilian side, where no such measure exists. Picture two markets with the same budget. On the left, five companies split it evenly. On the right, one company gets 80 percent. That second market is what we call concentrated.

data.title: The data: every federal contract action since FY2008
data.source: Source: USAspending.gov Award Data Archive, contracts, all agencies, release of 2026-09-06.
data.takeaway: Each row says who bought what, from whom, for how much, and whether others could bid. Adding up rows by buyer, product and company shows who wins the money.
data.notes: We downloaded the government's public archive: 18 yearly files and 88.8 million rows. Each row is one contract action. Here is a real one from July 2025: Veterans Affairs paid Optum, part of UnitedHealth Group, 857 million dollars for managed healthcare, and the contract was openly competed. Keep this one in mind: we come back to this market at the end.

process.title: How we turned 18 zip files into a trusted dataset
process.takeaway: Every number we show traces back to the published files, and our totals agree with the government's own official figures.
process.notes: Before analysing anything, we made sure the data is right. One: we checked every file against its checksum and locked it. Two: we converted the files to a fast format and proved the copy is exact, row by row, to the cent. Three: 62 quality checks on every row found the records that would distort the measure, such as a 13.9 billion dollar entry reversed the next year. Four: we built the analysis tables, and 116 checks confirm they add back to the original. Our yearly totals match GAO's official figures within 0.2 percent.

segment.title: How we measure: segments, and a score for each
segment.takeaway: A segment is one market: one buyer, one kind of product, one year. Its score says how much of that market's money went to the top companies.
segment.notes: We cut the spending into segments. A segment is one agency buying one kind of product in one year. For example: Veterans Affairs buying managed healthcare in FY2025. In that segment, 75 companies shared 22.8 billion dollars, and the largest got 98 percent. Each segment gets a score, the HHI, the standard antitrust measure. Square each company's percentage share and add them up. Five equal companies score 2,000. One company with 80 percent scores 6,500. One company with everything scores 10,000. Above 2,500 counts as highly concentrated. Our VA example scores 9,680, near the top.

trend.title: Finding 1: half of civilian money is concentrated
trend.dipSegment: contractors operating its buildings and sites
trend.takeaway: Since FY2014, a growing share of civilian contract money goes to markets where a few companies win most of it, while civilian contract spending doubled.
trend.notes: To turn 18 years of segments into one number per year, we add up the dollars in all segments scoring above 2,500 and divide by all civilian contract dollars. In FY2025 that is 152 billion of 301 billion, or 50 percent. In FY2008 it was 44 percent. It moved between 38 and 44 percent until FY2014, climbed to 53 percent in FY2022, and is at 50 percent now. Why the dip in FY2024? Mostly one Department of Energy segment: contractors operating its buildings and sites, about 17 billion dollars, scored below 2,500 that year. That one segment explains 15 of the 19 billion dollar drop. Also worth knowing: one in three civilian segments has a single company, but those are small purchases, only about 4.5 percent of the money. The concentrated money is in big markets.

where.title: Finding 2: Veterans Affairs leads, in health care
where.takeaway: Veterans Affairs is the largest civilian buyer, and 76% of its money now sits in highly concentrated segments. Three of its health segments put $44B with one company each.
where.notes: Which agencies? This chart shows, for the six largest civilian agencies, how much of each one's money sits in highly concentrated segments, in FY2008 and FY2025. Veterans Affairs jumped from 33 to 76 percent, and it is the largest civilian buyer at 78 billion dollars. GSA doubled, from 17 to 36 percent. Energy, HHS and NASA went down. On the right, the three biggest concentrated civilian segments in FY2025 are all VA health care: managed healthcare, 22.8 billion, 98 percent to UnitedHealth Group. Drugs, 11.7 billion, 98 percent to McKesson. Government health insurance, 9.5 billion, all to TriWest. Together, 44 billion dollars where one company gets almost everything.

example.title: Example: how one VA market became concentrated
example.takeaway: In six years this market grew almost 60 times larger and went from 167 companies with no clear leader to one company with 98% of the money.
example.notes: Here is the VA managed healthcare market over time. The grey bars are the money, the orange line is the largest company's share. In FY2019 it was a small market: 389 million dollars, 167 companies, and the largest had 19 percent. Then it grew very fast. By FY2025 it was 22.8 billion dollars, and one company, UnitedHealth Group, had 98 percent. Remember the contract on the data slide: it was openly competed. So concentration is not the same as a lack of competition. Our data shows what happened, not why, and that is the kind of question the next phase will look at.

next.title: What it means, and what we do next
careful: One big contract can swing a year
next.takeaway: Half of civilian contract money now goes to markets where a few companies win most of it. Next we test which rises are real and what they have in common.
next.notes: To sum up. The data is solid: our copy is exact, it matches GAO, and product codes carry across the 18 years. Two cautions: one big contract can swing a single year, and when we test trend lines, many apparent rises happen by chance, so we need a rule that separates real rises from noise. Next we set that rule, link the product codes that changed, settle our data decisions with our sponsor, and then ask what the markets that became concentrated have in common. Thank you.

backup_defense.title: Backup: civilian and Defense follow a similar path
backup_defense.note: Defense is about 60% of contract dollars. Its FY2024 dip comes from combat ships and fixed-wing aircraft, which fell below 2,500 that year and came back in FY2025.
backup_defense.notes: For context, Defense and civilian agencies have followed a similar path, both ending near 50 percent in FY2025.

backup_kind.title: Backup: civilian services are where concentration grew
backup_kind.note: Kind of purchase from the product code: codes starting with a digit are products, A is research, other letters are services.
backup_kind.notes: For civilian agencies, the growth is in services: their concentrated share rose from 37 to 48 percent while service spending more than doubled. Research is highly concentrated throughout.

backup_decisions.title: Backup: the data decisions barely change the picture
backup_decisions.note: V1 applies the decisions as proposed: reversal pairs replaced by their net, the two US Mint rows, MISCELLANEOUS FOREIGN AWARDEES and rows with no vendor ID left out. V8b also leaves out deobligations larger than the award's obligations that year.
backup_decisions.notes: With the proposed data decisions, under 1 percent of segments change band over 18 years. The trend only moves in FY2008 to FY2010. V8b needs flags from a pipeline step that is still running.

backup_codes.title: Backup: product codes mostly carry across the code changes
backup_codes.note: Product code manuals changed on 2011-10-01 and 2020-10-01. Codes that stopped at either change held almost no dollars. New codes took 87% construction and repair in FY2012, and almost all IT in FY2021.
backup_codes.notes: Old codes were almost never retired. New codes were added and some spending moved onto them, mostly construction in FY2012 and IT in FY2021. We will link those codes across the changes.

backup_noise.title: Backup: yearly swings are larger than the 500-point cutoff
backup_noise.note: A line is one agency and one product code, FY2012 to FY2020, with at least 6 scored years and $10 million. Shuffling keeps each line's yearly scores and drops their order, so it shows what noise alone produces.
backup_noise.notes: At a 500-point cutoff, 38 percent of lines rise and 28 percent still rise with their years shuffled, so most apparent rises are noise.

backup_features.title: Backup: some fields change coverage over time
backup_features.note: Set-aside and offers fields are blank on many dollars from FY2018, and most of the blank rows are orders under contract vehicles. The order competition field is blank on 75% to 88% of dollars, since it applies only to some orders.
backup_features.notes: Sole-source share is stable at about a third of dollars. Two fields change coverage in FY2018, which matters for explaining concentration later.
